background_notes.fact: For s>0 and finite δ>0, the infimum of the nonnegative covering costs in M001 on ℝ^m at scale δ equals H^s_δ(A) in D002. Countable covers and ℕ-indexed covers give the same costs, and their real versus extended diameter conventions agree at this scale.

grounds.reason: On a bounded Euclidean set its extended diameter is the embedded finite real diameter; all admissible members have diameter at most δ.
D002 uses countable covers, diameter bound ≤δ, positive exponent, and zero cost for empty members.
M001 uses sequences, the same diameter bound, and zero cost for empty members.
The argument fixes Euclidean A, assumes s>0, and compares an arbitrary finite positive scale.

background_notes.justification: Embed the finite nonnegative diameters into [0,∞]; positive real powers of finite values agree with their extended counterparts, including 0^s=0. Thus corresponding cover members have equal costs. Enumerate a countably infinite cover bijectively by ℕ; pad a finite or empty family with empty members. Conversely a sequence is a countable indexed family. Reindexing a nonnegative sum preserves it, since the sum is the supremum of finite subsums, and inserting zero terms preserves those suprema. The admissible cost sets therefore have equal infima.

background_notes.fact: Let C(r) be the M001 infimum of cover costs at scale r∈(0,∞]. For 0<r≤t≤∞, C(r)≥C(t). Consequently sup_{r∈(0,∞]} C(r)=sup_{δ∈ℝ,δ>0} C(δ), with finite scales embedded in [0,∞].

grounds.reason: The only dependence of admissibility on r is diam(T_k)≤r; all infima and suprema take values in [0,∞].
The proof compares the extended-scale supremum with all finite positive real scales.

background_notes.justification: Every r-admissible cover is t-admissible for r≤t, so the infimum over the smaller collection is at least that over the larger. Every positive finite extended scale is the embedding of a positive real. The supremum over all scales is at least the finite-scale supremum. In the reverse direction all finite-scale terms are bounded by that supremum, and C(∞)≤C(1), which is also bounded by it. These order comparisons prove equality without interchanging limits or assuming an infimum is attained.
